n: King Hezekiah falls deathly ill, and the prophet Isaiah brings a hard message: get your affairs in order, because you will not recover. This story is told again in Isaiah 38 and 2 Chronicles 32.

f.g: Make final arrangements for your family and kingdom—settle who inherits and what should be done.

n: Hezekiah turns his face to the wall—shutting out everyone else in the room—and pours his heart out to the Lord in private prayer.

f.w: turned his face to the wall
f.g: A gesture of privacy and earnestness; he turns away from the people around his bed to speak only to God.

n: Hezekiah reminds the Lord of his faithful life and weeps bitterly. His prayer is honest and emotional, a model of bringing real feelings to God.

f.g: A whole, undivided heart—sincere loyalty, not sinlessness.
Wept bitterly; “sore” means intensely.

n: Before Isaiah has even left the palace courtyard, the Lord speaks to him again. The quick answer shows how closely God was listening to Hezekiah’s prayer.

f.g: Before.
Probably a central courtyard of the royal palace (some ancient copies read “middle city”).

n: The Lord sends Isaiah back with tender words: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Hezekiah will be healed and go to the temple in three days to give thanks.

f.w: I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears

f.g: Leader or prince of God’s people.

n: God promises fifteen more years of life and protection for Jerusalem from Assyria. The city is defended for the sake of God’s own name and His covenant with David.
Isaiah prescribes a fig poultice for the king’s inflamed sore. God often works through ordinary means like medicine alongside miracles.

f.g: A cake of pressed figs, used in the ancient world as a poultice to draw out infection.
An inflamed sore or ulcer, perhaps a symptom of a deadly infection.

n: Hezekiah asks for a sign to confirm the promise—not out of doubt so much as a desire for assurance that he will really live to worship at the temple.
Isaiah offers a choice: should the shadow on the stairway move forward ten steps or back ten steps? The sign will show that God controls even time and the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew ma‘alot—steps; likely a staircase whose steps marked the sun’s shadow like a clock.

n: Hezekiah reasons that a shadow moving forward is natural, so he asks for the harder sign: let it go backward.

f.g: An easy or ordinary thing.

n: Isaiah prays and the Lord turns the shadow back ten steps on the stairway Ahaz had built. The text does not explain how; it simply testifies that God did it.

f.g: Literally “the steps of Ahaz,” a structure built by Hezekiah’s father that worked as a sundial.

f.w: brought the shadow ten degrees backward

n: Babylon’s king sends envoys with gifts after hearing of Hezekiah’s recovery. Babylon was then a rising rival to Assyria, likely hoping to recruit Judah as an ally.

f.g: Also spelled Merodach-baladan (Isaiah 39:1), a Chaldean ruler who repeatedly rebelled against Assyria.

n: Flattered, Hezekiah gives the envoys a full tour of his wealth and weapons. Showing off his resources to a foreign power was both prideful and politically unwise.

f.g: Showed.
The royal armory, where weapons were stored.

n: Isaiah confronts the king with probing questions. Hezekiah answers proudly that the visitors came from far-off Babylon, as if that made the visit an honor.

f.g: Babylon was hundreds of miles away; Hezekiah seems impressed that such a distant power sought him out.

n: Hezekiah admits he showed them everything. His openness to Babylon contrasts with his earlier humble prayer to the Lord.

f.w: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shewed them

n: Isaiah prepares to deliver a solemn message from the Lord.

f.w: Hear the word of the LORD

n: Isaiah prophesies that the very treasures Hezekiah displayed will one day be carried to Babylon. This was fulfilled over a century later when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem.
Some of Hezekiah’s own descendants will be taken captive and serve in Babylon’s palace. Daniel and his friends, young nobles of Judah, were among such captives.

f.g: Palace officials or servants; the Hebrew word can mean a court officer, not always a castrated man.

f.w: the palace of the king of Babylon

n: Hezekiah accepts the judgment as just, while expressing relief that peace will last in his lifetime. Readers often see this as a mix of humility and short-sighted comfort.

f.g: Peace and security; “truth” here carries the sense of stability and faithfulness.

n: The narrator mentions Hezekiah’s great engineering work: a tunnel bringing water from the Gihon spring into Jerusalem. That tunnel still exists today and can be walked through.

f.g: Hezekiah’s Tunnel, about a third of a mile long, cut through rock to protect the city’s water during siege.

n: Hezekiah dies and is succeeded by his son Manasseh, who would become one of Judah’s most wicked kings—a painful turn after such a faithful father.

f.g: A gentle idiom for death; he joined his ancestors.
